frictionVectors.title: European energy dependence
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains strong bargaining power as a major gas supplier, but European efforts to diversify imports could gradually reduce its leverage. Hydrocarbon dependence also limits broader economic sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel and border insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Instability across Mali, Libya, and Niger pressures Algeria’s security perimeter and complicates its non-interventionist regional posture.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic corridor rivalry
frictionVectors.details: The Lobito Corridor is attracting United States, European, and Chinese interest because of its role in moving copper and cobalt from the interior. External financing and operators could constrain Angola’s long-term control over critical transport infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and petroleum exposure
frictionVectors.details: Oil revenues remain central to fiscal stability, while past borrowing and infrastructure ties to Chinese lenders continue to narrow policy flexibility.

frictionVectors.title: Niger pipeline and trade dispute
frictionVectors.details: Benin’s role as an outlet for Nigerien crude and regional trade is vulnerable to diplomatic tensions, border restrictions, and changing military authorities in the Sahel.

frictionVectors.title: Jihadist spillover
frictionVectors.details: Armed groups operating from Burkina Faso and Niger are increasing pressure on northern Benin, threatening transport routes, agricultural zones, and state access to frontier resources.

frictionVectors.title: Diamond-market concentration
frictionVectors.details: Botswana’s fiscal model remains exposed to global diamond demand and its commercial relationship with De Beers, despite efforts to secure better national value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and water constraints
frictionVectors.details: Limited domestic power and water capacity may increase reliance on regional suppliers and foreign capital as Botswana develops new mineral and industrial projects.

frictionVectors.title: Gold control and smuggling
frictionVectors.details: The military government is seeking greater state control over gold production and marketing, but insurgent-held zones, informal mining, and cross-border smuggling limit effective sovereignty over the sector.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security dependence
frictionVectors.details: Expanded reliance on Russian security assistance may reduce Western influence while creating new dependencies around arms, mining access, and political support.

highlights: Mining ambitions constrained by weak governance

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda–Burundi Security Rivalry
frictionVectors.details: Mutual accusations over armed-group support and border insecurity continue to disrupt trade and constrain coordinated management of regional resources.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Mining Chain
frictionVectors.details: Gold and rare-mineral activity remains vulnerable to opaque licensing, smuggling, and external trading networks, limiting state capture of resource rents.

highlights: Tourism and aid remain structural dependencies

frictionVectors.title: Atlantic Port Competition
frictionVectors.details: Cabo Verde seeks to expand port, logistics, and digital-connectivity roles while balancing European, Chinese, and other external commercial interests.

frictionVectors.title: External Energy Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Fuel imports and dependence on external finance leave the archipelago exposed to shipping disruptions and foreign control of critical infrastructure.

highlights: Oil and gas revenues remain externally mediated
Infrastructure corridors are strategic pressure points

frictionVectors.title: Chad–Cameroon Pipeline Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The pipeline and export terminal provide vital revenue but preserve strong foreign operational and financial leverage over Cameroon’s petroleum sector.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese Infrastructure Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed roads, dams, and industrial projects expand infrastructure capacity while increasing exposure to debt, contractor, and strategic-access pressures.

highlights: Security partnerships trade access for protection

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security–Mining Nexus
frictionVectors.details: Russian-linked security actors retain substantial influence around regime protection and mineral sites, weakening transparent state control over mining revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Borderland Resource Smuggling
frictionVectors.details: Gold, diamonds, timber, and livestock move through porous borders, with armed groups and neighboring commercial networks capturing value outside formal state systems.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Revenue and Pipeline Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chad’s fiscal sovereignty remains tied to oil exports through the Cameroon corridor, leaving revenue collection vulnerable to foreign operators and regional disruption.

frictionVectors.title: External Security Partnerships
frictionVectors.details: The government is diversifying security relationships after reducing reliance on France, but foreign military and political backing continues to shape strategic decision-making.

frictionVectors.title: Mayotte and maritime sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: The unresolved dispute with France over Mayotte remains the central sovereignty issue, affecting migration, maritime jurisdiction, and diplomatic relations.

frictionVectors.title: External financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: Infrastructure and budget support rely heavily on France, Gulf partners, and China, limiting Moroni's room to set independent investment priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Conflict and mineral corridors
frictionVectors.details: Armed-group activity and regional tensions continue to weaken Kinshasa's control over eastern territory and mineral routes, while neighboring states and foreign networks face accusations of benefiting from informal trade.

frictionVectors.title: Mining contract sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: Copper, cobalt, and other strategic minerals attract Chinese, Gulf, and Western competition, but weak enforcement and opaque subcontracting limit the state's ability to capture full value.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign oil operators retain major influence over production and revenues, leaving Brazzaville exposed to price shocks and constraining diversification.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-linked infrastructure leverage
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed roads, ports, and energy projects improve connectivity but increase dependence on external contractors, financing terms, and commodity-linked repayment capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Cocoa sovereignty gap
frictionVectors.details: Cote d'Ivoire has improved domestic regulation and processing ambitions, but international buyers and volatile global prices still capture much of the value generated by cocoa exports.

frictionVectors.title: Port and strategic investment competition
frictionVectors.details: Abidjan and San Pedro are attracting French, Chinese, Gulf, and other foreign capital, creating growth opportunities while raising concerns over long-term control of logistics infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign military footprint
frictionVectors.details: U.S., Chinese, French, Japanese, and other military facilities provide revenue and security but constrain Djibouti's strategic autonomy and make the country vulnerable to regional rivalry.

frictionVectors.title: Port and debt exposure
frictionVectors.details: Control of major port and logistics assets is central to national sovereignty, while debt obligations and dependence on Ethiopian trade create leverage for external lenders and partners.

highlights: Suez revenue under Red Sea pressure

frictionVectors.title: Nile Water Security
frictionVectors.details: The GERD dispute with Ethiopia remains unresolved, leaving Egypt exposed to upstream water-management decisions and regional bargaining pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capital Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Gulf investment, IMF-linked reforms, and asset sales provide liquidity but increase outside influence over ports, land, and strategic infrastructure.

highlights: China remains a critical infrastructure partner

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Falling oil and gas output constrains fiscal sovereignty, while foreign energy firms retain substantial influence over production and technical capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Infrastructure Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-built infrastructure has expanded state capacity but increased dependence on external financing, contractors, and opaque resource-backed arrangements.

highlights: Red Sea position gains strategic value
Mining remains the main foreign-exchange engine

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea Militarization
frictionVectors.details: Regional conflict and competition around ports and shipping lanes increase pressure on Eritrea to accommodate external security interests while preserving its non-aligned posture.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concentration
frictionVectors.details: Industrial mining provides revenue but leaves the country dependent on a narrow set of foreign operators, commodity prices, and export corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Economic Dependence on South Africa
frictionVectors.details: Trade, transport, electricity, and financial links with South Africa give Mbabane limited room to pursue fully autonomous economic and infrastructure policy.

frictionVectors.title: Sugar and Manufacturing Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Export industries remain vulnerable to external market access rules, regional supply chains, and foreign-owned capital, limiting domestic control over value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Nile Basin Confrontation
frictionVectors.details: The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam increases Ethiopia's leverage over regional electricity and water politics but continues to generate acute tensions with Egypt and Sudan.

frictionVectors.title: External Finance and Strategic Assets
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring, IMF-linked reforms, and foreign investment needs may improve stability while limiting policy autonomy over currency, telecommunications, and infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Concession Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The post-transition authorities are seeking greater state participation and local processing in oil and manganese, creating tension with established foreign operators and investors.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign capital remains central to port, rail, and mining logistics, limiting Libreville's ability to fully control strategic export infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Senegambia Border and Fisheries
frictionVectors.details: Cross-border trade, fishing access, and security cooperation with Senegal remain essential but periodically generate sovereignty concerns and local resentment.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Energy Constraints
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia remains dependent on external financing for port modernization, electricity, and fuel security, leaving key infrastructure exposed to donor and investor priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Illegal Mining and Foreign Networks
frictionVectors.details: Illegal gold mining continues to damage water systems and undermine state authority, with foreign-backed trading and equipment networks complicating enforcement.

frictionVectors.title: Debt, Lithium, and Raw Exports
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and IMF conditions constrain policy space while Ghana negotiates how to capture more value from gold, bauxite, oil, and emerging lithium production.

frictionVectors.title: Simandou Corridor Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Simandou iron-ore project is expanding state revenues but ties Guinea's strategic autonomy to foreign-led rail, port, and financing arrangements.

frictionVectors.title: Bauxite Governance and Transition
frictionVectors.details: Foreign mining dominance and limited domestic processing remain major sovereignty concerns, while the military government's political transition increases uncertainty over contracts and oversight.

highlights: Fragile State at the Maritime Edge

frictionVectors.title: Cashew Trading Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The economy relies heavily on raw cashew exports, leaving farmers and public finances vulnerable to foreign buyers, price shocks, and weak domestic processing capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Port, Fisheries, and Security Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Weak maritime enforcement and dependence on external support create vulnerabilities around fisheries access, port development, and illicit trafficking routes.

highlights: Ports and Critical Minerals in Play

frictionVectors.title: External Debt and Fiscal Leverage
frictionVectors.details: IMF-backed fiscal reforms and large debt-service obligations limit Nairobi's room to negotiate infrastructure and resource agreements on fully sovereign terms. Public resistance to taxation and austerity complicates implementation.

frictionVectors.title: Lamu Corridor and Mineral Competition
frictionVectors.details: The Lamu port and related transport corridor remain exposed to regional insecurity and uneven commercial viability. Foreign investors are also positioning around Kenya's emerging critical-minerals and energy sectors.

frictionVectors.title: Highlands Water Project Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho's fiscal position and infrastructure planning remain closely tied to water exports and project arrangements with South Africa. This creates revenue but limits bargaining autonomy over a nationally strategic resource.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Mining Value Chains
frictionVectors.details: Diamond production depends heavily on foreign capital, technology, and marketing networks. Limited domestic processing means much of the value and strategic leverage remains outside Lesotho.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concessions and Local Value Capture
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, gold, and other mineral projects are dominated by multinational operators, leaving Liberia reliant on concession revenue and vulnerable to disputes over jobs, taxation, and environmental obligations. Efforts to renegotiate terms face investor and fiscal pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Mining corridors, rail access, and port facilities are essential to export earnings but are shaped by foreign operators and lenders. Weak domestic infrastructure reduces the state's ability to capture downstream value.

frictionVectors.title: Competing Claims over Oil Institutions
frictionVectors.details: Libya's divided political authorities continue to contest control over budgets, appointments, and oil-linked revenues. Production and export stability remain vulnerable to blockades, militia pressure, and institutional fragmentation.

frictionVectors.title: External Military and Energy Influence
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Russia, Egypt, the UAE, and European actors retain overlapping security and energy interests in Libya. Foreign-backed security arrangements and commercial deals constrain the country's ability to consolidate independent control over its infrastructure and coastline.

highlights: Nickel and Cobalt under Foreign Control

frictionVectors.title: Large-Scale Mining Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Nickel, cobalt, ilmenite, and other minerals are developed primarily through foreign-financed projects, exposing Madagascar to commodity cycles and external corporate leverage. Domestic processing and fiscal capture remain limited.

frictionVectors.title: Power, Roads, and Port Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Unreliable electricity and weak transport links increase dependence on foreign investors and development finance for strategic infrastructure. This dependence can narrow the government's negotiating space over mining and export corridors.

frictionVectors.title: External Debt and Policy Conditionality
frictionVectors.details: Malawi remains dependent on IMF-backed reforms and creditor negotiations, limiting near-term policy autonomy. Fiscal consolidation and currency adjustments are politically and socially difficult.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Minerals and Power Constraints
frictionVectors.details: The government is seeking greater value from uranium, rare earths, and other mineral assets, but foreign capital and weak electricity infrastructure constrain local control over production.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Bamako relies heavily on Russian-linked security support while reducing cooperation with France and other Western partners. This improves regime latitude but increases external dependence and operational opacity.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Nationalism and Gold Revenue
frictionVectors.details: Authorities are pressing foreign miners for larger state participation and revenue shares, especially in gold. Disputes over permits, taxes, and operating conditions risk investment disruption and production losses.

frictionVectors.title: Greater Tortue Ahmeyim Revenue and Governance
frictionVectors.details: Offshore gas production with Senegal offers Mauritania new fiscal and geopolitical leverage, but revenue-sharing, local-content, and transparency expectations remain sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Energy and Minerals
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, offshore gas, and prospective green-hydrogen projects depend on international operators and infrastructure finance. Nouakchott is seeking stronger domestic participation without deterring strategic investors.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos Sovereignty and Security Arrangements
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius continues to manage the sovereignty question over the Chagos Archipelago while navigating the security importance of Diego Garcia. The issue tests its ability to secure recognition without sacrificing strategic leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Financial-Center External Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius retains strong institutional capacity, but its offshore financial sector remains exposed to international tax, transparency, and anti-money-laundering standards shaped abroad.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara Recognition Contest
frictionVectors.details: Rabat uses diplomatic, infrastructure, and investment ties to consolidate its position in Western Sahara. The dispute continues to shape relations with Algeria, Spain, the Sahel, and major external powers.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capital in Strategic Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Gulf, European, and U.S. investment supports ports, automotive manufacturing, renewables, and logistics. Morocco generally preserves policy control, but strategic assets remain exposed to competing external interests.

highlights: Cabo Delgado Remains a Sovereignty Test

frictionVectors.title: Foreign LNG Consortiums
frictionVectors.details: Large offshore gas projects remain central to Mozambique's fiscal ambitions but depend on foreign capital, technology, and security guarantees. Delays and renegotiations continue to limit national control over the value chain.

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado Insurgency
frictionVectors.details: Militant violence continues to threaten communities, gas infrastructure, and transport corridors. External military and private-security assistance improves protection but underscores the state's dependence on outside actors.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Oil Ownership
frictionVectors.details: Major discoveries have attracted international oil companies and heightened expectations for local participation, taxation, and downstream processing. Namibia is seeking stronger state leverage without deterring investment.

frictionVectors.title: Green Hydrogen Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed hydrogen and ammonia projects could diversify the economy, but financing, water access, transmission, and export infrastructure may leave Namibia bearing risks while external investors capture much of the value.

frictionVectors.title: Uranium Concessions
frictionVectors.details: Relations with former Western operators have deteriorated as the junta seeks greater control over uranium and other mining assets. New partnerships with non-Western actors could increase bargaining power but bring financing and technical uncertainties.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline and Export Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Crude exports rely on regional pipeline access and politically exposed transit arrangements. Border insecurity and strained relations with neighboring states raise the risk that infrastructure access becomes a source of external leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Oil Finance
frictionVectors.details: Production recovery and new investment depend heavily on international capital, technology, and insurance. Contract reform is improving state leverage, but insecurity, theft, and revenue leakage continue to weaken effective sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Refining and Energy Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: New domestic refining capacity could reduce dependence on imported fuels and strengthen Nigeria's strategic autonomy. Pipeline vandalism, grid weakness, and regulatory disputes remain major constraints.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern Congo Mineral Flows
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's regional security posture and alleged links to mineral flows from eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo continue to generate diplomatic and sanctions pressure. Kigali denies exploitative conduct and frames its role around border security.

frictionVectors.title: External Security Partnerships
frictionVectors.details: Foreign military cooperation and peacekeeping deployments provide revenue, influence, and operational reach. They also expose Rwanda to reputational risk and accusations that security capabilities serve regional economic interests.

frictionVectors.title: OFFSHORE EXPLORATION
frictionVectors.details: International interest in the country's offshore blocks has not yet produced commercial discoveries. São Tomé and Príncipe remains exposed to unfavorable licensing terms and limited technical capacity.

frictionVectors.title: GULF OF GUINEA SECURITY
frictionVectors.details: Illegal fishing and maritime crime threaten fisheries revenue and food security. The country relies heavily on regional and external partners for patrol capacity and maritime monitoring.

highlights: Oil and gas era begins under scrutiny

frictionVectors.title: HYDROCARBON CONTRACTS
frictionVectors.details: Production from the Sangomar oil field and Greater Tortue Ahmeyim gas project is strengthening state revenues, but foreign operators retain major technical and financial leverage. Contract transparency, cost recovery, and domestic participation remain politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: FISHERIES AND PORT CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: Industrial fleets and foreign fishing agreements continue to generate tension with coastal communities. Dakar is also balancing external investment in ports and logistics against demands for greater national control.

highlights: Strategic maritime position attracts competing partners

frictionVectors.title: EXTERNAL SECURITY FOOTPRINT
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles depends on India, France, and other partners for maritime surveillance, coast-guard support, and anti-piracy operations. This improves security while creating sensitivities over strategic access and alignment.

frictionVectors.title: FISHERIES AND TOURISM DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-owned or foreign-linked tuna operations and tourism supply chains capture substantial value outside the archipelago. Climate exposure and limited domestic capital constrain efforts to deepen local ownership.

frictionVectors.title: IRON ORE AND RUTILE DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale mining remains dominated by foreign capital and vulnerable to commodity-price swings. The government is pressing for revenue, local procurement, and environmental safeguards while negotiating from a position of limited technical and fiscal capacity.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND RAIL INFRASTRUCTURE
frictionVectors.details: Mining-linked rail and port projects can expand export capacity but risk functioning as dedicated corridors with limited economy-wide benefits. Chinese and other external financiers retain significant influence over project terms and implementation.

highlights: Offshore resources are becoming a sovereignty contest
Ports and security remain externally shaped

frictionVectors.title: OFFSHORE OIL LICENSING
frictionVectors.details: Federal and regional authorities face disputes over licensing authority, revenue sharing, and the legal basis for exploration. Foreign oil companies and neighboring states can exploit institutional fragmentation while Somalia lacks the capacity to independently supervise offshore operations.

frictionVectors.title: PORTS AND SECURITY PARTNERSHIPS
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Gulf states, and other partners provide critical military, port, and logistics support, but their agreements can deepen rivalries among Mogadishu, federal member states, and Somaliland. Al-Shabaab, piracy risks, and contested maritime access continue to limit autonomous resource control.

frictionVectors.title: Rail, Port, and Power Bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Chronic weakness at Eskom, Transnet, and freight corridors limits sovereign control over energy and mineral exports. Private concessions and foreign capital are increasingly necessary to restore capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Minerals Pressure
frictionVectors.details: The United States, China, and European partners are competing for platinum-group metals, manganese, and rare-earth supply chains, testing Pretoria's effort to retain domestic processing and policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Sudan Pipeline Dependency
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan's oil exports depend on infrastructure crossing war-torn Sudan, leaving revenue and production vulnerable to sabotage, transit bargaining, and external security actors.

frictionVectors.title: Elite Capture and Armed Fragmentation
frictionVectors.details: Political factionalism and armed networks divert oil income and weaken national control over territory, infrastructure, and border trade.

frictionVectors.title: Gold and War Economies
frictionVectors.details: Competing armed authorities and foreign-linked trading networks are extracting value from gold and agricultural corridors, while formal institutions lose control over export revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Port Sudan Strategic Competition
frictionVectors.details: The Red Sea coast and Port Sudan draw competing Gulf, Russian, Egyptian, and Western interest, increasing the risk that infrastructure access becomes tied to military and commercial concessions.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Financed Corridor Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Gulf, and Western partners are competing for influence over railways, ports, and logistics corridors, creating financing options but also long-term leverage over strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: LNG and Mining Bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Natural-gas and critical-mineral projects offer major fiscal gains, but contract terms, local-content demands, and environmental disputes will determine whether value remains domestically controlled.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Logistics Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Lomé's role as a regional transshipment and trade hub attracts Turkish, Chinese, Gulf, and European commercial influence, making customs, concessions, and supply-chain control strategically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel Spillover Risk
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity and instability moving south from Burkina Faso threaten northern transport routes and may increase reliance on external security assistance.

frictionVectors.title: EU migration and financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: European funding and migration cooperation give the EU substantial leverage over Tunisian policy. Fiscal stress limits Tunis's room to reject externally conditioned support.

frictionVectors.title: Energy import vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on Algerian gas and imported energy exposes Tunisia to regional supply and pricing pressures, while domestic phosphate disruption constrains export earnings.

highlights: Oil development advances under external capital

frictionVectors.title: East African Crude Oil Pipeline
frictionVectors.details: The Uganda-Tanzania pipeline remains central to Kampala's energy strategy but faces financing, environmental, and diplomatic pressure from Western actors. Uganda retains formal ownership interests while relying heavily on foreign operators and lenders.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese financing and contractors remain important for roads, power, and industrial projects. Debt-servicing obligations and project guarantees can narrow Uganda's policy autonomy.

highlights: Debt restructuring trades autonomy for relief

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: Copper and cobalt attract intense competition among Chinese, Western, Gulf, and regional investors. Zambia is seeking more local processing and value capture but remains dependent on external capital and technology.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and transport constraints
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring has improved fiscal space but increased scrutiny from creditors and international financial institutions. Reliance on routes through Tanzania, Namibia, and Zimbabwe creates logistical and political vulnerabilities.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals concessions
frictionVectors.details: Zimbabwe is tightening controls on raw mineral exports and seeking domestic beneficiation, particularly for lithium. Chinese companies remain prominent in mining, leaving Harare balancing investment access against concerns over value leakage.

frictionVectors.title: Sanctions and monetary vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Western sanctions, restricted financial access, and persistent currency instability limit Zimbabwe's bargaining power with investors. The government increasingly relies on non-Western partners and mineral-backed economic relationships.
